question: Is it established that about 95% of enterprise generative-AI pilots deliver no measurable return?

framing.restatement: Is it established that approximately 95% of enterprise generative-AI pilots produce no measurable return?
scope_in: The provenance, wording, and intended population of the approximately 95% claim
How enterprise generative-AI pilots and measurable returns are defined and counted
Reported pilot outcomes, measurement methods, and observation periods
The distinction between returns not measured, returns not detected, and measured zero or negative returns
Whether the reported findings describe a particular sample or support a broader enterprise-wide prevalence claim
scope_out: Whether generative AI is generally useful or valuable
Whether generative AI causally improves enterprise performance
Predictions of future pilot success rates
Recommendations about whether a particular enterprise should invest in generative AI
presuppositions: Enterprise generative-AI pilots can be identified as a population with a meaningful denominator.
Measurable return can be operationally defined over a specified observation period.
The approximately 95% figure refers to an observed or estimated frequency, rather than merely a rhetorical characterization.
A pilot's lack of documented return is not necessarily equivalent to its producing no return.
framing.answerhood: A complete answer would give a qualified verdict on whether the approximately 95% prevalence claim is established, identifying its source, denominator, definition of return, observation period, and reported estimates and uncertainty. It would distinguish findings about a particular sample from claims about enterprise pilots generally, and distinguish unmeasured or undetected returns from measured zero or negative returns.

candidates.title: Effect of blending Jersey and Holstein-Friesian milk on Cheddar cheese processing, composition, and quality.
candidates.snippet: The effect of Jersey milk use solely or at different inclusion rates in Holstein-Friesian milk on Cheddar cheese production was investigated. Cheese was produced every month over a year using nonstandardized milk consisting of 0, 25, 50, 75, and 100% Jersey milk in Holstein-Friesian milk in a 100-L vat. Actual, theoretical, and moisture-adjusted yield increased linearly with percentage of Jersey milk. This was also associated with increased fat and protein recoveries and lower yield of whey. The composition of whey was also affected by the percentage of Jersey milk, with lower whey protein and higher whey lactose and solids. Cutting time was lower when Jersey milk was used, but the cutting to milling time was higher because of slower acidity development. Hence, overall cheesemaking time was not affected by the use of Jersey milk. Using Jersey milk increased cheese fat content in autumn, winter, and spring and decreased cheese moisture in spring and summer. Cheese protein, salt, and pH levels were not affected. Cheese was analyzed for texture and color, and it was professionally graded at 3 and 8mo. The effect of Jersey on cheese sensory quality was an increase in cheese yellowness during summer and a higher total grading score at 3mo in winter; no other difference in cheese quality was found. The study indicates that using Jersey milk is a valid method of improving Cheddar cheese yield.
